title: Job, batch and flow production, and choosing a method
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Know the features of job, batch and flow production, weigh their benefits and limitations, and recommend an appropriate method for a given situation.

blocks.heading: Job, batch and flow production compared
blocks.text:
Job production makes one item at a time to the customer's own specification, and one worker or team carries the job from start to finish: an Omatumba Metalworks gate made to one farmer's measurements, a bride's dress, a fitted kitchen. Batch production makes a group of identical items in one run, then resets the line for the next group: a Gobabis bakery makes 300 white loaves, then 200 brown, then 150 seed loaves from the same ovens. Flow production sends the product continuously along a line of stages, each doing one operation, and suits one standardised product in very large volumes: cement at an Ohorongo plant, bottled beer, refined sugar.

The choice trades unit cost against flexibility. Job gives exactly what each customer asked for and the craftsmen who see a job through tend to be motivated by it - but every item is different, so skilled (and expensive) labour is needed throughout and the cost per unit is the highest of the three. Batch spreads the set-up cost across the run and keeps some variety - each run differs only in colour, size or recipe, so the business sells a range without retooling the whole works - but while the line is reset between batches it produces nothing, and variety is limited to what one set of machines can make. Flow is the cheapest per unit and the fastest, but it produces only one standardised product, the machines need huge investment, and a fault at one stage can stop the whole line.

A quick test places any product on that range: ask how many different things the customer can order, and how many of each are wanted. One unique item points to job; a choice of varieties in their hundreds points to batch; one design in its thousands points to flow. A second question follows: how big is each order compared with the cost of setting up to make it - because a method earns its keep only when the run is large enough to repay what it costs to arrange.

blocks.heading: Choosing a method for a given situation
blocks.text:
The recommendation follows from the order pattern, and the chain runs in steps. Condition: if the product is one-off and made to one customer's specification - a gate, a ship's engine - then only job production can deliver it, whatever the cost. Where the market wants a range of varieties of the same product in moderate quantities - loaves in three recipes, paint in twelve colours - batch is the fit, because the same machines make each variety and resetting between runs is affordable if each run is large enough. Mechanism: when volumes are high and the product standardised, flow production drives unit cost down, because the enormous set-up cost is spread over thousands of identical units and each stage runs without stopping. Consequence: the business that matches method to market tends to combine competitive unit costs with the variety its customers demand - and where it misjudges, the effect is a cost too high for the price, or a range the customer did not want.

Because the three methods are not mutually exclusive in real businesses, a manufacturer can run job work alongside batch runs; the recommendation for a given situation names which the main volume belongs to.

The recommendation is also reversible evidence: when a business finds itself resetting its machines every hour, that is batch work being forced through at flow volumes, and the misfit shows up as changeover time in the cost of every unit - just as a standard product dragged through job work shows up as wasted craft hours on identical items. Reading the method off the order book, and the order book off the method, is how a recommendation is checked after the event.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Unit cost, which the method chosen largely determines, is priced and broken down in topic 4.2, and the scale at which flow becomes affordable is the economies-of-scale story there. The quality consistency that flow and automation buy is examined in 4.3. The workers displaced or re-skilled by automation and training are the human-resource concerns of 2.2, and the cash freed by lean stock control appears in 5.1.
